video_title: Tariffs & Protectionism: Investing Needs a New Set of Rules | Luke Gromen Explains
gist: Luke Gromen argues the US has formally abandoned neoliberalism for 'Hamiltonian economics' (tariffs, industrial policy, a neutral reserve asset), a regime shift he rates as big as the fall of the Berlin Wall or Nixon closing the gold window, and that the arithmetic of 120% debt/GDP with a ~4.7% 10-year ceiling forces secularly negative real rates. His positioning: 5-25% physical gold replacing bond duration, cash for optionality, electrical-infrastructure and industrial equities, non-US equity weight in Japan/Germany/Poland/Hungary, and skepticism that hyper-valued AI companies survive Chinese price competition.

insights.claim: US policy has formally shifted to 'Hamiltonian economics' — high tariffs, protection of domestic industry, and a neutral reserve asset — a 180-degree reversal of the globalization/neoliberal regime that governed markets since roughly 1982.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Every backtest built on the 1982-2020 disinflation regime is being run against the wrong rulebook; reposition toward the prior regime's losers.
insights.quote: In a nutshell, Hamiltonian economics are high tariffs protect protection of domestic industry and a neutral reserve asset.

insights.claim: The policy shift is officially signposted, not speculative: US Trade Representative Jameson Greer said at Davos the US is going back to Hamiltonian economics and cited the Hamilton paper, and Treasury Secretary Bessent said the same in a speech at the America 250 gala at the New York Economic Club and in a same-day Wall Street Journal op-ed.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Treat tariffs and industrial policy as a durable multi-year framework rather than negotiating tactics that get reversed.

insights.claim: The regime change is bipartisan and therefore survives elections: Biden did more than Trump 1.0 on semiconductor sanctions, and domestic manufacturing construction spending grew orders of magnitude faster under Biden than under Trump's second term so far.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Don't underwrite a mean-reversion-to-free-trade trade on the next election; the political variable is a figurehead, not a policy switch.
insights.quote: when you go from someone like Trump to someone like Biden and the policy doesn't change and then you go back to Trump again and the policy doesn't change. That's just your figurehead king.

insights.claim: The US Treasury bond cannot remain the world's reserve asset under a reshoring policy, because a country cannot simultaneously export dollars and financial assets in exchange for goods and also make the goods itself.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Implies structurally lower foreign bid for Treasuries and a rising role for a neutral asset — the core structural bull case for gold.
insights.quote: if we start making more stuff, ultimately, our deficits are going to have to be resolved in something other than Treasury bonds in particular and in financial assets more broadly.

insights.claim: Reshoring is being driven by a national-security imperative rather than economics — the US borrows from China to build weapons to face down China using Chinese components, a risk the Joint Chiefs chairman Admiral Michael Mullen flagged back in 2011.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Security-motivated policy is price-insensitive, so expect subsidies, price floors and government equity stakes in critical industries to persist through cost overruns.
insights.quote: We're borrowing money from China to build weapons to face down China using Chinese components.

insights.claim: Reversing the offshoring of production to China must be reflationary by definition, since the offshoring itself was demonstrably disinflationary.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Structurally higher inflation floor argues for real-asset and pricing-power exposure over nominal fixed income.
insights.quote: If if offshoring all of this stuff that China was disinflationary, which we know it was, by definition, reversing it has to be reflationary.

insights.claim: Wall Street still does not accept that neoliberalism is dead, making the Hamiltonian shift a genuinely non-consensus positioning input.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: If the view is right and un-priced, the repricing of commodities, industrials and gold has years left to run.
insights.quote: The Washington has changed its view of neoliberalism. It's dead. And that's still I think a very controversial or certainly not a consensus view amongst uh Wall Street and most investors.

themes.theme: The 4.7% Ceiling and Negative Real Rates

insights.claim: The US fiscal structure cannot tolerate a 10-year yield much above roughly 4.6-4.8%, and when the 10-year hit 4.7% again Treasury intervened in markets in a way it hadn't in 40 years.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Treat ~4.7% on the 10-year as a policy-reaction trigger level: approaching it should be traded as a liquidity-injection and dollar-weakening catalyst.
insights.quote: We can't afford rates above X. And then you say, "Okay, well, whatever X is and it seems to be roughly 4. You know, I've been saying 4.6 to 4.8% on the 10-year."

insights.claim: The bulk of the nominal rise in Treasury yields is likely finished (roughly 1.5% to 4.8% on the 10-year), but the US is only in the first or second inning of secularly negative real rates.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Long bonds may not crash nominally but should be structurally avoided as a real-return asset; own the assets that benefit from falling real rates.
insights.quote: I think we're in like inning one or two of negative real rates.

insights.claim: Stocks should soar in dollar terms over the next 5-10 years while losing in gold terms — since the Fed began hiking in 2022 the S&P is up roughly 50-70% in dollars but down about 25% measured in gold.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Nominal equity bullishness and real-terms bearishness can coexist; benchmark portfolios in gold to see whether you are actually compounding.
insights.quote: in real terms, stocks are losing money. I think they're going to keep losing in real terms, but in in dollar terms, I think they're going to soar.

insights.claim: Deeply negative real rates are the historically proven mechanism for cutting US debt/GDP: after WWII the ratio fell from 110%+ in 1946 to 50-55% by 1951 via capital controls, significant inflation, and real rates that bottomed at -13%.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: The template implies bondholders get expropriated in real terms; the historical playbook also includes capital controls, which few portfolios are positioned for.
insights.quote: Capital controls, significant inflation, and real rates in the United States that bottomed at -13%. Thank you for your service, long-term Treasury holders.

insights.claim: Gromen's 2021 client study found that taking US debt/GDP from 130% to 80% over five years — assuming debt/GDP keeps growing 8% a year as it has on average since 2008 — would require real rates of -12% for five straight years.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of financial repression required; anything less means the debt problem persists and the debasement trade keeps running.
insights.quote: we could do it. We just needed to have real rates be -12% to five straight years.

insights.claim: The US mathematically cannot repay its debt in nominal terms and will default unless real rates get secularly more negative or an improbable productivity boom occurs that raises output without reducing employment, since about half of federal receipts come from employment.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Frames AI-driven white-collar job destruction as a fiscal negative, not just a productivity positive — the two scenarios that 'save' the debt are mutually contradictory.

insights.claim: The market is in the 'bargaining' stage of a five-stage grief process about US fiscal reality — stablecoin T-bill demand, BOJ/yen intervention and FIMA swap lines are the bargains being proposed — with depression and acceptance still ahead.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Each new plumbing fix is a sentiment rally to sell rather than a structural solution; the acceptance phase is where real rates go deeply negative.

insights.claim: The 'debasement trade is dead' narrative of the last three months is wrong; if Hamiltonian policies are being pursued across administrations, the debasement trade must run for a minimum of 5 to 10 more years.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Treat debasement-trade drawdowns as adds rather than trend breaks while the policy regime holds.
insights.quote: We've been hearing in the last 3 months the debasement trade's dead. It's not close to dead.

insights.claim: US veterans benefits have gone from roughly zero at the start of the Iraq war to a $400 billion-a-year liability growing at 8-10% annually — two to three times the growth rate of tax receipts — now consuming about 8% of receipts.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: An under-modeled, non-discretionary spending line compounding faster than revenue; it tightens the fiscal math independent of rates.
insights.quote: as a parting gift we have now have a $400 billion a year asbestos liability in the form of veterans benefits that are growing two to three times tax receipts.

insights.claim: The US is spending over 100% of tax receipts on just three items — interest, entitlements and veterans benefits — all of which are growing faster than receipts even with receipts at all-time highs.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Everything discretionary, including defense and industrial policy, is deficit-financed by construction — the mechanical case for monetization.

insights.claim: Strip the American flag off the fiscal profile — 120% debt/GDP, 6% deficits heading to 7-8%, lost wars, exploding entitlements — and investors would unanimously short the bonds and the currency, as they do with Brazil or Argentina.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A country-blind screen is a cheap bias check; the same logic flags the UK and, to a lesser extent, France.
insights.quote: I'm going to take the country flag off the off the masthead. 120% debt to GDP multiple dumb wars

themes.theme: Gold as Duration and the Fugger Portfolio

insights.claim: Investors should hold at least 5-10% in physical gold and replace their bond duration with physical gold for the time being.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A concrete, sizeable allocation shift away from the standard 60/40 with token or zero gold weight.
insights.quote: I think 5 to 10% everyone should have in physical gold, I think, number one. And I would just replace your duration with physical gold for the moment.

insights.claim: Inflation-adjusted returns on long sovereign bonds averaged -1% per year over the 80 years from 1901 to 1981, meaning the 1982-2020 bond bull market that trained everyone alive today is the historical anomaly, not the norm.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Any 40-year backtest justifying bond allocations is sampling the exception; extend the lookback before sizing duration.

insights.claim: Gold works as the real-return yardstick because it tends to return 1-2% above actual inflation over time, and countries in fiscal and debt trouble systematically understate reported inflation.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Deflating portfolio returns by gold rather than CPI changes the ranking of asset classes and exposes hidden real losses.
insights.quote: just show me gold

insights.claim: Gold price suppression is far harder in a multipolar world because a surplus-running China that buys gold physically drains London and New York vaults, so manipulation eventually runs out of metal.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Structural change in gold's price-discovery mechanism — the post-1990s suppression regime is not the right base case going forward.
insights.quote: you can manipulate gold a little, but you can't manipulate it too much cuz you'll run out of gold.

insights.claim: The Jacob Fugger portfolio — 25% gold, 25% cash, 25% real estate, 25% blue-chip dividend equities, rebalanced — makes an investor 'unkillable' because it survives both tails, hyperinflation and long deflationary depression, and is the basis for Ray Dalio's All Weather.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A tail-neutral benchmark to measure your own allocation against; the survival logic, not the CAGR, is the point.
insights.quote: at that point that portfolio makes you unkillable as an investor over the long run

insights.claim: In genuine hyperinflation real estate does not protect you — it collapses to cash value unless it is productive land like timberland or farmland producing a commodity — while equities roughly keep up with inflation and cash evaporates.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Corrects a widespread assumption about real estate as an inflation hedge; favors productive land over generic property.
insights.quote: Real estate in a real hyperinflation collapses to cash value, but at least there's value there, particularly if it's timberland, farmland, something producing a commodity.

insights.claim: Gromen personally holds over 25% in gold and close to 20% of liquid net worth in T-bills, deliberately trading some upside for optionality because he has extremely high conviction in the destination but increasingly low conviction in the path.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Skin-in-the-game sizing plus an explicit path-vs-destination framework: hold dry powder to buy volatility rather than maximizing exposure to the thesis.
insights.quote: I have extremely high conviction in the destination of where we're going, and I have increasingly low conviction in the in the path to get there.

insights.claim: Gold fell from roughly 5,300 to 3,900 over the past four months, illustrating why an all-in gold position is dangerous even for a gold bull and why cash optionality also finances a zero-yielding gold holding.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Path volatility in gold is large enough to force sizing discipline; a T-bill sleeve turns drawdowns into buying opportunities.
insights.quote: And what's happened in gold over the last 4 months is a perfect example. 5,300 to 3,900 pretty quickly.

insights.claim: Buffett's dismissal of gold reflects survivorship luck — being born in America in 1932 near the bottom — and Buffett himself wrote around 1978-80 that all of Berkshire's businesses had underperformed gold by about 2% a year for roughly 15 years.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Undercuts the standard authority argument against gold and dates the conditions — dumb wars, guns and butter, currency devaluation — under which gold beats operating businesses.
insights.quote: all of our business, all of our employees, all of the economic value add, and a pet rock beat us for like 15 years

insights.claim: Portfolios with a meaningful real-asset sleeve expressed through gold were by far the most consistent producers of positive returns per decade going back 100 years to the 1920s, at a cost of only about 50 basis points of CAGR versus a 90% equity portfolio.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Quantifies the price of tail protection as small; the real cost of the 90% equity portfolio is a potential 70-80% real drawdown along the path.

insights.claim: US grid electricity generation in 2023 was the same as in 2004 — flat for 20 years while nominal GDP soared — which Gromen reads as direct evidence of financialization and a shift to service jobs rather than genuine real growth.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Flat generation is a 20-year backlog; reshoring plus AI demand implies a multi-decade capex cycle in grid and generation.
insights.quote: the United States grid generation in 2023 was the exact same as it was in 2004.

insights.claim: Electrical generation is the single best indicator of a country's real economic growth, and China went from under half of US generation in 2003 to nearly 2x today.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Use generation growth as a cross-check on official GDP; the US/China ratio is the cleanest single metric on relative industrial capacity.
insights.quote: if you said, Luke, you can have one indicator tells real economic growth of a country, what is it? And it's absolutely electrical generation.

insights.claim: The electrical infrastructure theme is not merely an AI derivative — it would sell off if AI sells off but the underlying reshoring-driven demand runs for the next 5 to 10 to 15 years regardless.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: An AI-correlated drawdown in grid names would be a buying opportunity rather than a thesis break, since the demand driver is separable.
insights.quote: It's not just AI. I think it gets hit if AI gets hit, but I'm not worried about it. It's I I think we are in open field running for the next 5 to 10 to 15.

insights.claim: Gromen has recommended the GRID and PAVE ETFs to clients for nearly four years as the vehicle for the electrification and infrastructure theme, with no commercial relationship to either.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A specific, investable expression of the thesis and a screen for individual names within it.

insights.claim: Industrial companies like Eaton, Parker Hannifin, Danaher and Illinois Tool Works sit in the middle of the grid buildout and should get both volume demand and pricing power as the US reverses 20 years of grid-capacity stagnation.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Names the specific business models — pricing power in a capacity-short market is the margin driver, not just unit growth.

insights.claim: Copper sits at the intersection of inflation, infrastructure and reshoring, alongside aluminum, stainless steel and silver, and the market still is not positioned for it.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A basket of electrification metals is the commodity-side expression of the Hamiltonian shift, and it remains under-owned.
insights.quote: copper's right at the intersection of that, right? Like inflation, infrastructure, and people just still aren't really there

insights.claim: Bob Farrell's rule — that in secular change markets play by new rules while most participants still use the old ones, and by the time everyone adopts the new rules it is mostly over — is the frame for today: long bonds are certificates of confiscation, gold is duration, commodities and industrials are back.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A timing frame: early-days positioning in the new regime is where the excess return is, and crowding is the exit signal.
insights.quote: in times of secular change, the markets will be playing by a new set of rules while most market participants are still investing or playing by the old rules

insights.claim: With US equities at roughly 70% of global market cap — echoing Japan at 50-60% in the late 1980s — excess returns will require owning something outside America, with a suggested shape of cutting US equity to about 50%, 15% in Japan, and 5% sprinkled across EM.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A concrete de-concentration template; the pitch is comparable returns at lower vol from not being in the consensus trade, not massive outperformance.
insights.quote: excess returns accrue to those who are not positioned like everybody else

insights.claim: America cannot reshore alone because it can no longer make the machines that make the machines, so it needs Japan, Germany or China — and with China excluded, capital flows toward Japan, Germany, Poland and Hungary as the countries that still make things.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific geographies that capture US reshoring spend — a non-obvious second-order beneficiary trade with a 10-year horizon.
insights.quote: America can't reshore because we can't make the machines to make the machines.

themes.theme: AI: Fiscal Drag and Chinese Price Competition

insights.claim: AI is a fiscal negative in the near term: the companies are borrowing heavily and competing with Bessent for capital, pushing up Treasury borrowing costs, while simultaneously threatening the white-collar jobs that generate roughly half of US tax receipts.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A second-order channel most AI bulls ignore — the more AI succeeds, the sooner the fiscal crisis and monetization arrive, which loops back into the debasement trade.
insights.quote: what AI is doing is borrowing money competing with Bessent to undermine the tax base of Scott Bessent

insights.claim: AI will repeat the telecom fiber pattern: the infrastructure is real and hugely productive, but most of the companies laying it go to zero and the buyers of the assets out of bankruptcy become wealthy.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Be the second mouse — the trade is on the distressed asset acquirers and downstream users, not on the current capex spenders.
insights.quote: the early bird gets the worm but the second mouse gets the cheese

insights.claim: Chinese-model token usage on OpenRouter has gone from roughly 3% to 45-50% in the last 18 months, per a Bloomberg chart, though OpenRouter is reportedly only 2-3% of total token spend.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: An early, imperfect but fast-moving tracker of Chinese AI share; a caveated leading indicator for US AI pricing power.

insights.claim: Having watched Chinese competition play out from Cleveland over 20 years, Gromen says the sequence always runs 'it's not as good' to 'it's close' to 'it's cheaper and better' — and once you reach the last stage it is already over.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: A pattern-recognition template for handicapping Chinese entry into any industry, now being applied to AI model pricing.
insights.quote: And if you get to that last oh god, it's cheaper and better, it's already over. You're done.

insights.claim: Valuation is arbitrary and irrelevant until something changes — and the mere existence of a serious debate about Chinese AI competitiveness on price is fatal to businesses trading at 1,000x, 100x, 10x, and probably even 5x sales.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: The de-rating trigger is a change in narrative, not a change in fundamentals; watch the debate itself as the signal for AI multiple compression.
insights.quote: Valuation doesn't freaking matter. Throw it in the trash. But valuation doesn't matter until something changes. Then valuation starts to matter

insights.claim: The first 'gates' on AI capital are already coming down: OpenAI and Anthropic have restricted secondary-market trading of private stock, with the threat that unauthorized secondary sales may void the stock, because a down round would unwind the entire structure.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Restricted price discovery in private AI marks means public-market comparables and index-level AI exposure are the only honest pricing mechanism; watch for further protectionist gating under national-security framing.
insights.quote: they're closing the gates on secondary trading for open AI and Anthropic. Saying, if you do if you secondarily trade secondary market your private open AI or Anthropic stock, it may void your stock.

insights.claim: Model commoditization is the boring bear case: the leading frontier models increasingly return the same answers to the same questions, so a cheap open-source Chinese equivalent is a serious risk to US AI economics.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: If frontier capability converges, differentiation collapses to price and distribution — bad for the capex-heaviest model developers.
